title: Victim's death a 'surprise'
article: "It was chaos from the time I entered (the ambulance) to the time I left," Const. Dean Ross testified Thursday at the fourth day of a coroner's inquest.
Vernon Dale Crowe died July 10, 2001 about 20 minutes after entering an ambulance for assessment following an epileptic seizure.
Paramedic Jason Williams made three calls for police help when the 32-year-old man abruptly went from agreeable to aggressive.
Ross, who got the call at 5:37 p.m., was the first officer to arrive in front of Souls Harbor Mission, where Crowe volunteered and ate supper.
He saw Williams and emergency medical technician Danae Ackles wrestling with their patient. "The man was in quite a fit of rage," Ross said.
In earlier testimony, Ackles recalled Crowe screaming "too hot," "need help" and "get out" in a struggle to exit the ambulance.
Ross didn't recall arriving with his pepper spray in hand -- contrary to the testimony of paramedics -- but admitted it was possible given the paramedics' distress call.

Realizing he couldn't get Crowe's flailing arms to the back to handcuff, Ross opted to cuff him in the front. But Crowe continued thrashing, he said. He grabbed Crowe's hair and also had a knee on his shoulders at some point in an effort to control him.

When Crowe "dragged his teeth" across the officer's forearm, Ross pushed Crowe's head back with the heel of his hand, striking his jaw area, he testified. Crowe head-butted the officer. Ross reacted by pulling his pepper spray from his belt and firing a "quick burst" at Crowe's face.
"It was an easy decision to use the pepper spray at that point. It was automatic," Ross, a 13-year constable, said.
"Pepper spray is so low on our use of force scale," he later added, explaining spray is preferable to physical blows.
When pressed by Crowe family lawyer Darren Winegarden about seeking advice from paramedics before spraying their patient, Ross replied: "After I've been head-butted, I can't just sit there."
Ross worried he might be knocked out if hit again -- leaving his sidearm vulnerable. "I have to assume the worst," he said.
Immediately after Crowe was sprayed, Williams injected him with a sedative but he continued fighting, witnesses said.
Within seconds, three other paramedics and four additional police officers arrived. Ross exited the ambulance.
A former junior hockey league player in the 1980s, Ross said his 90 seconds with Crowe left him "exhausted."
Const. Todd Wall said he tried to handcuff Crowe's legs, but realized it wouldn't work. He and a paramedic instead wrapped gauze bandage around the man's ankles to control them.

Asked to explain marks around Crowe's ankles in autopsy photos, Wall admitted they didn't appear consistent with the bandage. Winegarden suggested they looked more like handcuff marks, but Wall said he didn't believe his cuffs ever touched Crowe's legs.

Some witnesses were asked if Crowe was ever "hog-tied," and they all said no. About 10 minutes after the additional officers arrived, Crowe -- lying on his stomach and now cuffed behind his back -- had no pulse.
The inquest continues today.
